results.title: Weighted Kappa in R: Best Reference - Datanovia
results.content: ## Weighted Kappa in R: For Two Ordinal Variables. In biomedical, behavioral research and many other fields, it is frequently required that a group of participants is rated or classified into categories by two observers (or raters, methods, etc). The analysis of the agreement between the two observers can be used to measure the reliability of the rating system. In a previous chapter (Chapter @ref(cohen-s-kappa)), we described the classical *Cohen’s Kappa*, which is a popular measure of *inter-rater reliability* or *inter-rater agreement*. The Classical Cohen’s Kappa only counts strict agreement, where the same category is assigned by both raters (Friendly, Meyer, and Zeileis 2015). This chapter describes the **weighted kappa**, a variant of the Cohen’s Kappa, that allows partial agreement (J. In other words, the weighted kappa allows the use of weighting schemes to take into account the closeness of agreement between categories. Recall that, the kappa coefficients remove the chance agreement, which is the proportion of agreement that you would expect two raters to have based simply on chance.

results.title: Theory of Trust and Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence Technology (TrAAIT): An Instrument to Assess Clinician Trust and Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence - PMC
results.content: Our study set out to develop and assess a novel clinician-centered model to measure and explain trust and adoption of AI technology. In the fully moderated causal model, clinician trust explained a large amount of variance in their acceptance of a specific AI application (56%) and their post-adoption general trusting stance towards AI in general (36%). In this study, we set out to uncover trust and acceptance factors underlying clinician adoption in a novel model (TrAAIT) and validate its performance in a real-world setting. To address these gaps, our TrAAIT model was formulated to define, measure, and evaluate the behavioral determinants which explain a clinician’s relationship with, trust in, and willingness to use, AI-based technologies [4, 6–9, 12, 20, 32]. In our conceptual model, trust is the antecedent to a clinician’s acceptance of (i.e., willingness to use) AI-enabled applications as cognitive support. Our study demonstrates that the TrAAIT model is a novel, valid tool for understanding, predicting, and assessing clinician trust and adoption of AI technologies. The TrAAIT model explains a significant amount of variance in clinician acceptance of a specific AI application (56%) and their post-adoption trusting stance towards AI in general (36%). For application value, though rated above acceptable, the tool draws focus to addressing its ease of use which was scored unacceptable by the sample, MDs, and APPs. TrAAIT can be deployed at key checkpoints in an organization’s AI implementation pipeline to complement AI model evaluation with user perspectives on clinical relevancy, quality, organizational assurances, and adoptability. This study reports on the development and validation of a novel model, TrAAIT, for assessing clinician trust in AI applications. This study found that an AI-based application’s *information credibility*, *system performance*, and *application value* were the most potent factors that make up clinician trust and that trust predicted the user’s *acceptance* attitude (i.e., willingness to adopt) towards the specific AI-based solution. For these reasons, the new TrAAIT model can be a useful application to assess AI-based technologies in terms of the applications’ critical attributes that drive clinicians to trust, accept and adopt AI-based technology.

results.title: Enhancing Clinician Trust in AI Diagnostics: A Dynamic Framework for Confidence Calibration and Transparency
results.content: **Background:** Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven Decision Support Systems (DSSs) promise improvements in diagnostic accuracy and clinical workflow efficiency, but their adoption is hindered by inadequate confidence calibration, limited transparency, and poor alignment with real-world decision processes, which limit clinician trust and lead to high override rates. **Methods:** We developed and validated a dynamic scoring framework to enhance trust in AI-generated diagnoses by integrating AI confidence scores, semantic similarity measures, and transparency weighting into the override decision process using 6689 cardiovascular cases from the MIMIC-III dataset. This work adds significant contributions to the current available literature on AI transparency mechanisms, including a dynamic, multi-factor acceptance rule that integrates model-reported confidence, semantic similarity, and a length prior with transparency-conditioned thresholds that tighten when explanations are weaker—an explicit mechanism to calibrate clinician reliance on AI outputs; a formal scoring formulation that defines a composite trust score and a single-step acceptance rule, enabling transparent implementation and auditability; operational use of transparency as a gate modifier rather than a stand-alone predictor, so high self-ratings cannot compensate for low confidence or low similarity; a priori, transparency-specific parameters (weights and thresholds) fully specified for straightforward deployment and review; pragmatic text-quality constraints via a minimum similarity cut-point (0.10) and a length prior that gives full credit to 30–100-character diagnoses to discourage vague or list-like outputs; a large-cohort evaluation on 6689 MIMIC-III cardiovascular cases demonstrating a reduction in overrides from 87.64% to 33.29%, emphasizing workflow-relevant impact beyond discrimination metrics; stratified evidence that confidence is the dominant driver of acceptance while transparency and similarity chiefly shape borderline decisions; statistical robustness through 95% confidence intervals for overall and stratified override rates alongside association testing (χ 2 with Cramér’s V); and a full interaction analysis across confidence-by-transparency strata that clarifies when transparency meaningfully shifts decisions versus when confidence predominates. Override rates were analyzed across multiple dimensions to assess the impact of AI Transparency Level, Confidence Calibration, and Diagnostic Similarity on clinician acceptance. By combining model-reported confidence, semantic similarity between AI-generated and clinician-verified diagnoses, a length-based score, and transparency-conditioned thresholds, the current framework substantially reduced overrides relative to earlier iterations.

results.title: Weighted Cohen's Kappa: Measuring Inter-Rater Agreement
results.content: # Weighted Cohen's Kappa. Weighted Cohen's kappa is a measure of the agreement between two ordinally scaled samples and is used whenever you want to know if two people's measurements agree. In the case of a "normal" Cohen's Kappa, the variable to be measured by the two raters is a nominal variable. If you have an ordinal variable, that is, a variable in which the characteristics can be ordered, then of course you want to take that order into account. If you want to take the size of the difference into account, you have to use the weighted Cohen's Kappa. So if you have a nominal variable, you use Cohen's Kappa. If you have an ordinal variable, you use the weighted Cohen's kappa. It is important to note that the weighted Cohen's Kappa can only tell you how reliably both raters are measuring the same thing. Since we have an ordinal variable with the rank order dissatisfied, neutral and satisfied, we determine the agreement with the weighted Cohen's kappa.
